561.title: The rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31)
561.hook: a beggar at the gate has a name; the rich man doesn't
561.howItsDone: Christians read this parable when thinking about wealth and about those at their own gate, and some church outreach to people living on the street begins with learning names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mammon, and a shrewd manager praised for seeing that his time was short. Your line was faithful in little.

The man who sells the newspaper. The woman who cleans the office after everyone goes home. Someone by the same doorway each morning with a paper cup. Faces seen every day, with no names. Jesus tells a story about a gate and two men on either side of it. Only one gets a name, and it isn't the one you'd expect. Some readers point out that no other character in his parables is named at all.

In the King James Bible: "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day." Purple was the cloth of kings. "And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores." Laid there, as if someone carried him. He longs for crumbs from the table, and the dogs come and lick his sores. Lazarus is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, usually explained as God has helped. Nobody else is helping him. The rich man has no name at all; later tradition called him Dives, but that's just the Latin word for rich. Both men die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man is in torment. And here's the detail that stings. The rich man calls across: send Lazarus to cool my tongue. He knew his name. Every time he passed that gate, he knew who was lying there. The story never says he kicked or cursed him. He just didn't see him as someone his to help. Abraham answers that a great gulf is now fixed between them. The rich man begs for Lazarus to warn his five brothers. They have Moses and the prophets, Abraham says, and "neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead." Christians differ on how literally to read the afterlife scenes; some take them as a parable, not a map. Either way, the story starts at the gate. The gulf began there.
screen: then, large: `A CERTAIN BEGGAR NAMED LAZARUS.`

segments.voice: Picture your ordinary route through a day, the street, the shop, the bus, and let the faces you pass again and again come up one by one: the cleaner, the guard, the cashier with the tired smile. Notice whose names you don't know. If you pray, hold each of them before God, even without a name.
Lazarus, a Greek form of Eleazar, God has helped: the beggar at the gate, whose name the rich man knew all along.
Your line: the beggar had a name. Every face at the gate has one. Day five hundred sixty-one.

562.title: Faith like a mustard seed (Luke 17:1–10)
562.hook: the apostles ask for more faith; he says a mustard seed is enough
562.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the apostles' words, increase our faith, in times of doubt, and some churches teach that faith grows by acting on it in small daily obedience rather than waiting for certainty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus, the beggar at the gate whose name the rich man knew. Your line was the beggar had a name.

I need more. More faith, more certainty. If I just believed harder, I could do the hard thing. Some people of faith know that request well, and Luke shows exactly when the apostles make it. Not after a storm or a miracle. Right after Jesus gives them an instruction about forgiveness that sounds, frankly, impossible. Their reply is three words in the King James Bible, with nothing polished about it.

Here's the instruction: if your brother wrongs you, tell him; if he repents, forgive him. "And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him." Anyone who's lived with a sibling or a roommate knows how hard that is. So the apostles say: "Increase our faith." And Jesus doesn't. He answers: "If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you." A mustard seed is tiny. A sycamine is a full-grown tree. Uprooting it and planting it in the sea is a deliberately absurd picture. Readers hear this in more than one way. Some hear a gentle rebuke: you don't yet have even a seed's worth. Others hear encouragement: even a speck of real trust in God is enough to do impossible things, so you don't need more before you start. Then a short story that sounds harsh at first. A servant comes in from plowing, and his master doesn't say, sit down, let me serve you. The servant makes dinner first. So you too, Jesus says, when you've done everything you were told, say: "We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do." On that reading, forgiving seven times a day isn't a heroic feat that needs a giant supply of faith. It's the next job, done with a little faith. No medal. Just the work, and the seed doing what seeds do.
screen: then, large: `IF YE HAD FAITH AS A GRAIN OF MUSTARD SEED.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been putting off until you feel more ready, an apology, a forgiveness, a step in prayer, and notice the voice that says not yet. Picture a mustard seed, small enough to lose in your palm, and name the smallest first step you could take with what you've got. If you pray, say the apostles' words: increase our faith.
Mustard seed: the tiny seed Jesus names when the apostles ask for more faith, a speck that could uproot a tree.
Your line: increase our faith. An honest prayer, three words long. Day five hundred sixty-two, done.

563.title: Ten healed, one returned (Luke 17:11–19)
563.hook: ten lepers healed; only a Samaritan comes back to say thank you
563.howItsDone: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans, Lutherans and others call communion the Eucharist, the thanksgiving; in the United States, some churches read the story of the ten lepers around Thanksgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mustard seed of faith, enough to move a tree. Your line was increase our faith.

Between Samaria and Galilee, at the edge of a village, ten men stand at a distance. They have to. They have leprosy, the Bible's word for skin diseases that made a person unclean, and the law said they must live apart: no home, no work, no family's touch. At least one, we'll learn, is a Samaritan. Trouble has put them all on the same road. They see Jesus coming, and they don't come closer. They lift up their voices.

In the King James Bible they cry: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." He doesn't touch them or say be healed. He says: "Go shew yourselves unto the priests." The law required a priest to confirm someone had recovered. But they haven't, yet. They have to start walking while still sick. "And it came to pass, that, as they went, they were cleansed." Then the turn: "And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God, And fell down on his face at his feet, giving him thanks: and he was a Samaritan." The same loud voice he'd used to beg, now used to praise. Giving thanks, in Greek, is eucharisteo. Eu, good; charis, grace or gift. It's where the word Eucharist comes from, the name Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans and others use for communion, the great thanksgiving. Jesus asks: "Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?" To be fair, the nine were doing what they were told, heading to the priests. Luke never calls them ungrateful. But only one turned around and came back first. Jesus calls him "this stranger," a foreigner. The outsider is the one who sees the gift. Then: "Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole." All ten were cleansed. Some readers notice that only this one hears he's been made whole. The healing reached his skin. The thanks reached further.
screen: then, large: `THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last year to one good thing you received and walked on from: a recovery, a favor, someone who stood by you when they didn't have to. Picture yourself turning around on the road, and find the words you'd say to them. If you pray, turn back to God with the same thanks.
Eucharisteo, Greek for giving thanks, good grace: what the healed Samaritan did when he turned back, and the root of the word Eucharist.
Your line: where are the nine? One came back, and heard he'd been made whole. See you tomorrow.

564.title: The kingdom among you (Luke 17:20–37)
564.hook: the kingdom of God is within you, or in your midst
564.howItsDone: Christians pray thy kingdom come every time they say the Lord's Prayer, and some churches speak of the kingdom as both already present and not yet complete, especially in Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eucharisteo: ten were healed, and one came back giving thanks. Your line was where are the nine?

When? Some Pharisees put it to Jesus straight: when will the kingdom of God come? When will things be put right, and God's reign be plain to see? Under Roman rule, people longed for that day. It's a fair question. His answer is two verses long, and one tiny phrase in it can be read two ways.

In the King James Bible: "The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you." Not with observation: you can't track it like an astronomer watching for a comet. Don't chase people who say it's over here, or over there. Then the tiny phrase, in Greek entos hymon. It can mean within you, inside each person. That's how the King James reads it, and Leo Tolstoy took a book title from it. But it can also mean among you, in your midst, and other translations prefer that. Some readers point out that Jesus is speaking to people questioning him, and the one standing in front of them was Jesus himself. On that reading, the kingdom is already in the middle of you, and you're asking when. Christians hold both readings. Some stress the inner life: God's reign begins in the heart. Others stress the community and the person of Jesus: God's reign is happening right here, among people. Some hold the two together. Then Jesus turns to his disciples and talks about a day that will come as suddenly as lightning, while people are eating, drinking, marrying, planting, as in the days of Noah and of Lot. Three words of warning: "Remember Lot's wife." She looked back. The passage holds two things together: the kingdom is already here, and still coming. The question was when. The answer points to where: already in the room.
screen: then, large: `THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS WITHIN YOU.`

segments.voice: Look around wherever you are, at the people near you or their traces, a photo, a chair someone sat in, and notice where there's kindness, patience or peace, even a little. Then turn inward to one small good thing already growing in you; you don't have to make it, just notice it. If you pray, give thanks for it.
Entos hymon, the Greek phrase that can mean within you or among you: Jesus' answer to when the kingdom comes.
Your line: in your midst. Closer than the horizon, and still coming. Day five hundred sixty-four.

565.title: Of such is the kingdom (Luke 18:15–17)
565.hook: they bring even infants to be touched
565.howItsDone: Many churches baptize infants, including Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Reformed churches, while Baptists and many others hold services of dedication and blessing for babies and baptize those who profess faith for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, entos hymon: the kingdom within you, or among you, already here and still coming. Your line was in your midst.

A crowd around a famous teacher: serious men with serious questions about the law, the end of the age, money and the kingdom. And pushing in at the edges, parents carrying babies. Not toddlers who could ask questions. Babies, swaddled, asleep, maybe crying. All the parents want is for him to lay his hand on them. To the disciples, it looks like a distraction. You can almost hear them: not now, he's busy.

Matthew and Mark tell this too, and their children are paidia, young children. Luke changes one word. In the King James Bible: "And they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them." Infants. In Greek, brephe, babies. Luke used the same word for John the Baptist leaping in Elisabeth's womb, and for Jesus himself, the babe in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. These babies can't believe, or understand, or even ask to be brought. Then: "But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer, in old English, means allow. Let them come. Then the line that turns it on the adults: "Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child shall in no wise enter therein." What does a baby do? It receives. It's carried, fed, held. It doesn't earn anything. Luke puts this right after the tax collector who could only say God be merciful to me. The same point twice: the kingdom isn't achieved, it's received. Christians apply this differently. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize infants, and some read this passage at baptisms. Baptists and many others dedicate babies with a blessing and baptize those old enough to profess faith themselves. Both hear the same thing: the youngest are not a distraction. They're the model.
screen: then, large: `FOR OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child you know, your own, a niece, a neighbor's baby, or the child you used to be, and hold them in your mind as if carrying them toward someone who loves them. Wish them good things slowly: safety, kindness around them, room to grow. If you pray, pray for them by name; some families bless a child with a hand on the head or a sign of the cross at bedtime.
Brephe, Greek for infants, newborns: the babies the disciples tried to send away, and the ones Jesus says the kingdom belongs to.
Your line: as a little child. Nothing to earn, only to receive. That's day five hundred sixty-five.

566.title: One thing you lack (Luke 18:18–30)
566.hook: a rich ruler goes away sad; Peter says we've left everything
566.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns, and members of some Protestant communities, take vows of poverty in response to this call, while other Christians hear it as an invitation to hold possessions loosely and give generously.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brephe: babies carried to Jesus, and a kingdom received like a little child. Your line was as a little child.

Straight after the babies, who can do nothing, comes a man who has done everything right. Luke calls him a certain ruler: a leader, respected, wealthy. He's not trying to trap Jesus. He seems to really want to know: "Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" What shall I do. He's used to achieving things. He wants the list, right after babies who can do nothing.

Jesus first pushes back on the compliment: "Why callest thou me good? none is good, save one, that is, God." He names commandments: don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't bear false witness, honor your father and mother. And the man says, sincerely, "All these have I kept from my youth up." Then: "Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me." Not a longer list. A single loosening of the grip. "And when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich." Luke doesn't say he stormed off, or even left. He was sad. He seems to have wanted it, and couldn't let go. Then the hard saying: it's easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. You may have heard of a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle's Eye, where camels had to kneel. It's a nice sermon, but there's no ancient evidence for such a gate. Jesus seems to mean exactly what it sounds like: impossible. The listeners get it: "Who then can be saved?" And today's line: "The things which are impossible with men are possible with God." Peter, a little anxious: "Lo, we have left all, and followed thee." Jesus promises that no one who leaves house or family for the kingdom will miss out, now or in the age to come. Christians read the one thing differently. Some take it as this man's particular call. Others, like Antony of Egypt, who heard Matthew's version read in church, took it as their own and gave everything away.

segments.voice: Imagine being asked, gently, for the one thing you hold tightest: money, a home, a reputation, a plan for your life, a comfort you reach for every night. Don't argue with what comes up or try to give it up; just name it honestly, the way the ruler's sorrow was honest. Then rest in the line: what is impossible with men is possible with God.
Needle's Eye: a Jerusalem gate where camels supposedly knelt, with no ancient evidence behind it. Jesus' camel and needle simply mean impossible.
Your line: what is impossible with men. The rest of it: is possible with God. Day five hundred sixty-six.

567.title: What do you want? (Luke 18:31–43)
567.hook: a blind beggar at Jericho shouts, and Jesus stops the whole procession
567.howItsDone: Some Christians hear the blind man's cry, have mercy on me, in the Jesus Prayer that Orthodox Christians and others repeat, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me; the story is also read when praying for healing and for spiritual sight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich ruler, the one thing he lacked, and a Needle's Eye gate with no evidence behind it. Your line was what is impossible with men.

Just before Jericho, Jesus takes the twelve aside and tells them plainly what's coming in Jerusalem: he'll be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, killed, and on the third day rise again. And Luke adds an almost sad sentence: "And they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them." They have eyes. They've seen everything. And they can't see. Then, outside Jericho, they meet a man who has no eyesight at all.

Luke doesn't name him; Mark calls him Bartimaeus. He's begging by the roadside, hears a crowd, and asks what's happening. Jesus of Nazareth is passing. And he shouts, in the King James Bible: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Son of David is a title for the promised king. The man who can't see is the one who sees who Jesus is. The people at the front tell him to be quiet. "But he cried so much the more." Then: "And Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought unto him." A whole crowd on the road to Jerusalem, and it stops for one beggar. Then a question that sounds too obvious: "What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?" Jesus asks anyway, letting the man say it himself, as a person with a voice and not just a problem. "Lord, that I may receive my sight." The Greek verb can mean see again, and it can mean look up. "And immediately he received his sight, and followed him, glorifying God." Up the road to Jerusalem, toward everything the disciples couldn't understand. Look at the week: a beggar with a name, faith the size of a seed, one who turned back to give thanks, a kingdom in your midst, babies carried forward, a ruler who couldn't let go. And now a blind man who could see, a shout that stopped a crowd, and a question: what do you want?

segments.voice: Think of the voices around you asking for help, some loud, some quiet: a friend who keeps mentioning a hard time, a family member who calls too often. Imagine your day halting the way the crowd did, and asking one of them: what do you want me to do for you? Listen for their answer, not yours, and if you pray, ask for eyes to see who's calling.
Bartimaeus, the blind beggar outside Jericho, unnamed in Luke and named by Mark, whose shout stopped a whole crowd.
Your line: Jesus stood still. One voice was enough to stop him. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and another week on the path.
